newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin brings together warring defence chiefs.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin brings together warring defence chiefs.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, moving to assert his rule, summoned squabbling military chiefs to a joint public appearance on Friday with dire warnings of military decline from his defence minister ringing through the Kremlin.

The minister, Igor Rodionov, who according to the Russian media is engaged in a bitter battle with Yeltsin's chief defence adviser, Yuri Baturin, over military reform, said on Thursday night the country's armed forces were in a "horrifying state" of decay.

"No one today can guarantee the reliability of our control systems," he told invited Russian journalists. "Russia might soon reach the threshhold beyond which its rockets and nuclear systems cannot be controlled."
He had set out some of his fears in a letter to Yeltsin, recovering from pneumonia and heart surgery at his country residence, and Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.
Rodionov, 60, faces serious shortages of money for everything from arms purchases and maintenance to fuel and servicemen's pay.
But the timing of his remarks, on the eve of a joint appearance with Baturin, was clearly aimed at stealing the Kremlin defence aide's political thunder.

Yeltsin had summoned Baturin and Rodionov to a joint news conference intended to dispel any impression of top-level disarray in the sensitive area of national defence. The Kremlin expects the two to present a united front on reform policy.

Rodionov gave no details of his letter to Yeltsin. But in his comments to the Russian media representatives, he painted a picture of neglect of the nuclear arsenal and army which once contributed greatly to Moscow's superpower status.
His remarks signalled frustration at his inability to carry out reforms he promised when Yeltsin appointed him last July.

The Russian media have said Baturin, secretary of Yeltsin's Defence Council, believes reforms should be planned largely within the confines of the present military budget while Rodionov insists considerable extra funds are vital.

Reforms appear to have failed to get off the drawing board partly because of differences over how to carry them out and also because of Yeltsin's absence from the Kremlin for much of the last seven months, delaying many major decisions.
"Reform in the armed forces has turned into a struggle for their survival, a struggle against disintegration," Rodionov said.
"The whole horror is in the fact that, as Russian defence minister, I am becoming a spectator of the destructive processes in the army and can nothing about it."
Yeltsin was spending Friday at his country residence outside Moscow. He was expected to meet his chief aide Anatoly Chubais in the course of the day.
The Kremlin said on Friday that Yeltsin was considering the possibility of moving a March summit with U.S. President Bill Clinton from Washington to Europe.

The president's ill health has give rise to speculation that he would be reluctant to make the long journey to the United States. A European venue would allow Yeltsin to save face abroad and at home where he faces opposition charges that he is too weak to rule.
